title: How to Export Photos to MP4 Right in Your Browser
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Modern browsers can encode MP4 video locally. Here's how Reecap turns photos into a downloadable file.
description: How to export photos to MP4 in your browser using WebCodecs — no server, no upload. Reecap renders every frame locally and downloads a standard MP4.

body.text: You can export photos to MP4 directly in your browser using the WebCodecs API, which gives web pages access to the device's hardware video encoder. Reecap uses WebCodecs to render each frame on a canvas and encode an H.264 MP4 locally — no server and no upload.
How browser MP4 export works

For each moment in the timeline, the editor composites the background, the current and incoming photos with their transition, and any captions onto a canvas. That canvas becomes a video frame, which is fed to the hardware encoder and muxed into an MP4 in memory.
What you get

items: A standard MP4 (H.264) that plays everywhere.
720p (1×) or 1080p (2×) quality.
Your choice of aspect ratio: 16:9, 9:16, 1:1, 4:3, or 5:4.
Transitions and animations baked into the file.

body.text: Open the editor and export your photos to MP4.

faq.q: Can a browser export MP4 video?
faq.a: Yes. Modern browsers expose the WebCodecs API, which lets a page encode H.264 MP4 using the device's hardware encoder. Reecap uses this to export locally.

faq.q: Is browser MP4 export private?
faq.a: Yes. Because encoding happens on your device, your photos and the rendered video never leave your browser.

title: Video Transitions Explained: Fade, Slide, Zoom, and More
author: Rakibul Islam

description: Video transitions explained — fade, slide, slide up, zoom, wipe, flip, and dissolve — and when to use each in a photo recap. With examples you can try free.

body.text: A video transition is the visual effect used to move from one slide to the next. The most common transitions are fade, slide, zoom, wipe, flip, and dissolve, and each sets a different mood. Reecap offers eight transition styles you can set per slide.
Common transitions and when to use them

items: Fade — a soft crossfade; calm and cinematic.
Slide — pushes the next photo in; energetic and modern.
Slide Up — the next photo rises into frame; great for vertical video.
Zoom — scales in with a crossfade; adds momentum.
Wipe — reveals the next photo with a moving edge; bold.
Flip — a perspective turn; playful.
Dissolve — a blurred crossfade; dreamy.
None — a hard cut; punchy and fast.

body.text: Choosing transitions for a recap

Pick one or two transitions and stay consistent for a cohesive look. Use calm transitions like Fade and Dissolve for travel and memories; use Slide and Zoom for energetic social clips. In Reecap, transitions render into the exported MP4, not just the preview.

faq.q: What is the difference between fade and dissolve?
faq.a: A fade is a clean crossfade between two slides; a dissolve adds a slight blur during the crossfade for a softer, dreamier feel.

title: Making Photo Videos on Phone vs Desktop (in the Browser)
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: When to edit on mobile and when a bigger screen wins — and how the browser handles both.
description: Phone vs desktop for making photo videos in the browser: where mobile works, where a desktop wins for the timeline, and how Reecap handles each.

body.text: You can make a photo video in any modern browser on phone or desktop, but a bigger screen makes the timeline and side panels far easier to use. Reecap runs in the browser on both; for serious editing — reordering many slides, fine timing, dragging captions — a tablet or desktop is the better experience.
When mobile is fine
For a quick recap from a handful of photos, a phone browser works. You can add photos, pick a transition, and export. The constraint is screen space: the timeline and control panels need room.
When a desktop wins

items: Reordering and timing many slides on the timeline.
Precise caption placement by dragging.
Comparing transitions quickly.
Exporting larger projects.

body.text: Open the editor on whichever device you have — and reach for a bigger screen when you want more control.

faq.q: Can I make a photo video on my phone?
faq.a: Yes, in a mobile browser. For more control over the timeline and captions, a tablet or desktop is recommended.

faq.q: Do I need to install an app?

title: How Long Should a Recap Video Be?
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Ideal lengths for recaps by platform, and how to hit them with per-slide timing and speed.
description: How long should a recap video be? Aim for 8–15s on Reels/TikTok, under 60s for Shorts, and 20–40s for a year-in-review. Hit any length easily in Reecap.
keywords: how long should a recap video be

body.text: A recap video should usually be 8 to 15 seconds for Reels and TikTok, under 60 seconds for YouTube Shorts, and 20 to 40 seconds for a year-in-review. Shorter recaps hold attention better; the right length depends on the platform and how many photos you have.
Recommended lengths by use case

items: Instagram Reels / TikTok — 8 to 15 seconds.
YouTube Shorts — up to 60 seconds.
Feed posts — 10 to 20 seconds.
Year-in-review — 20 to 40 seconds.

body.text: Hitting your target length

Total length is the sum of your per-slide durations, divided by the speed. In Reecap, lower the per-slide duration or raise the speed to shorten a recap, and do the opposite to lengthen it. Preview playback shows the exact runtime.
Open the editor and dial in the perfect length.
